strengths: The paper combines Chain-of-Thought semantic decomposition with GRPO-based reinforcement learning for text-to-motion generation, a timely and potentially useful direction.
MotionCoT Data Engine automatically creates structured CoT annotations, reducing manual annotation cost and providing interpretable intermediate supervision.
The GRPO extension with format, motion-similarity, and semantic-similarity rewards is a reasonable adaptation of RL to motion token generation.
On HumanML3D, Motion-R1 achieves strong Diversity, MM-Dist, and competitive R-Precision, suggesting better semantic alignment and one-to-many generation.
Qualitative OOD examples show improved long-horizon and abstract prompt handling compared with a baseline.
The paper attempts an ablation study to isolate the contributions of CoT and the reward components.
weaknesses: Despite claiming evaluation on two benchmarks, no quantitative KIT-ML results are reported; only HumanML3D quantitative results appear in the main paper.
Table 1 labels baseline [9] as MotionLLM, while the rest of the paper identifies [9] as MotionAgent; this inconsistency raises concerns about baseline identity and evaluation credibility.

The method is not state-of-the-art in motion fidelity: FID 0.201 is far worse than MoMask (0.045) and MotionGPT-2 (0.191), and R-Precision@1 only ties the best baseline, so the SOTA claim is overstated.

The reward functions use pre-trained text/motion encoders from [3], which are also standard evaluation encoders for R-Precision, MM-Dist, and FID. Optimizing RL with the same encoders can directly inflate evaluation metrics and does not provide independent evidence.

The ablation study contains apparent duplicate rows and the text claims CoT alone is poorest, but the table shows a no-CoT variant with worse Top-1 and FID; component attribution is therefore unclear.
No comparison is made to relevant RL-based text-to-motion baselines such as MotionRL (PPO), nor to other CoT/planning-based motion generation methods.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code/model link, no hyperparameters such as group size, KL coefficient, clipping, or reward weights, no tokenizer architecture details, and no data-engine prompt or quality-control details in the main paper.
Out-of-distribution evaluation is qualitative only, with no quantitative OOD benchmark or human evaluation to support generalization claims.
The statement that GRPO avoids explicit reward functions contradicts the paper's use of multi-aspect reward functions; the RL formulation is described inconsistently.
The quality of LLM-generated CoT annotations is validated only by another LLM (DeepSeek-R1), with no human validation or downstream robustness analysis.
Ethical risks of text-to-motion generation, including misuse, deepfake motion, and bias in motion datasets, are not discussed.

strengths: The paper proposes a sensible combination of Chain-of-Thought reasoning with GRPO-based reinforcement learning for text-to-motion generation, targeting complex and compositional prompts.
The MotionCoT Data Engine is a practical idea for automatically generating structured CoT annotations with LLMs, reducing manual labeling cost and potentially improving interpretability.
Extending GRPO to motion generation with multi-aspect rewards is a reasonable direction, and the cold-start SFT strategy is technically plausible.
The HumanML3D experiments include confidence intervals, multiple baselines, and an ablation study, with some metrics clearly improved (e.g., R-Precision@2/@3, MM-Dist, Diversity).
Qualitative examples suggest the method can handle some out-of-distribution and abstract prompts better than a baseline, which is a useful direction for the field.
The paper is generally well organized and promised code/model/data availability supports reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: A central technical flaw: the motion similarity and semantic similarity rewards use the same pretrained text/motion encoders as the standard evaluation metrics (R-Precision, MM-Dist, etc.). Optimizing directly on the evaluator's embedding space can inflate these metrics without proving genuine motion quality, making the reported gains unreliable. No held-out evaluator, reward-model separation, or human evaluation is provided to address this.

The state-of-the-art claims are overstated. On HumanML3D, FID is 0.201, substantially worse than MoMask (0.045), T2M-GPT (0.116), and MotionGPT-2 (0.191); R-Precision@1 is not best; MModality is not best. The abstract and introduction claim across-the-board SOTA and multiple benchmarks, but the evidence is mixed.

Despite claiming evaluation on multiple benchmarks, only HumanML3D quantitative results are shown. KIT-ML is mentioned in the experimental setup but no KIT-ML results table or discussion is provided, so the multi-benchmark claim is unsupported.

Related RL-based baselines are missing. MotionRL, which uses PPO and multi-reward RL for text-to-motion, is cited but not compared experimentally. This is an important omission for positioning the GRPO contribution.

The ablation does not isolate the contribution of GRPO/RL training. There is no SFT-only or no-RL baseline, and several reward combinations are compared without clarifying what exactly is being optimized. This makes it difficult to attribute gains to the proposed RL component.

Novelty is incremental: the motion tokenizer is a standard VQ-VAE from prior work, GRPO is taken from LLM reasoning, and the reward functions are simple cosine similarities. The main new elements are the CoT data engine and the application of these ideas to motion generation, which is useful but not a deep technical advance.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper lacks key training details such as group size G, learning rate, batch size, KL coefficient, reward weighting, training time, and compute cost. It also does not report statistics or validation of the MotionCoT dataset generated by DeepSeek-R1.

The LLM-based CoT quality-control pipeline is not rigorously validated. Filtering by another LLM may introduce bias or noise, and no human verification, inter-annotator agreement, or manual analysis of CoT quality is provided.

Out-of-distribution generalization is only evaluated qualitatively with a few visualized examples. There is no quantitative OOD benchmark, user study, or controlled comparison, so the generalization claim is not convincingly supported.

The paper contains naming inconsistencies, e.g., MotionAgent vs. MotionLLM for citation [9], which causes confusion. There are also minor typos such as 'morbidity' likely intended as 'verbosity' in the data filtering description.

The abstract highlights small relative improvements in Diversity and R-Precision over one baseline while ignoring the FID regression relative to MoMask and others, giving a cherry-picked impression of the results.

strengths: The paper proposes Motion-R1, a unified framework that integrates Chain-of-Thought reasoning with GRPO-based reinforcement learning for text-to-motion generation, which is a timely and interesting combination.

The MotionCoT Data Engine offers an automated pipeline for generating structured CoT annotations, reducing manual annotation cost and providing interpretable intermediate reasoning for motion planning.
The method is evaluated on HumanML3D against a broad set of baselines, and it achieves competitive results on several metrics such as R-Precision@2/3, MM-Dist, and Diversity.
The ablation study attempts to isolate the contributions of CoT, semantic similarity reward, and motion similarity reward, providing some evidence for the design choices.
Qualitative visualizations on out-of-distribution prompts illustrate the potential of CoT-style decomposition for handling complex or abstract textual instructions.
weaknesses: The claim of state-of-the-art performance is overstated: FID is substantially worse than MoMask (0.201 vs. 0.045), R-Precision@1 is lower than MoMask, and MModality is not the best. Several reported gains are small and may not be practically significant despite confidence intervals.

The evaluation is incomplete: the paper claims multiple benchmark datasets but only provides quantitative results on HumanML3D in the main text. No KIT-ML quantitative results are shown, and out-of-distribution evaluation is only qualitative, without quantitative OOD benchmarks or user studies.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: applying CoT and GRPO to text-to-motion is an application of existing ideas, and related works such as MotionAgent (semantic planning) and MotionRL (PPO-based RL for motion) are not directly compared or sufficiently differentiated.

Reproducibility is limited: key details such as GRPO hyperparameters, reward weights, training time/compute, prompt templates, and motion-tokenizer training are missing or deferred to supplementary material. Code/model/data are promised but not yet available.

The method description lacks important clarity, including how CoT traces are used at inference, how motion tokens are decoded and evaluated, and how the reward functions avoid reward hacking or overfitting to pre-trained encoders.
The ablation table is confusingly formatted with ambiguous or duplicated rows, and ablations are only conducted on HumanML3D, not on KIT-ML or OOD settings, limiting the strength of the conclusions.

There is an inconsistency between the text referring to MotionAgent and the tables using MotionLLM for citation [9], which should be clarified. The paper also lacks discussion of broader ethical or misuse considerations for human motion generation.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: improving text-to-motion generation with reasoning-style decomposition and reinforcement learning.
Combines several modern components (LLM-based decomposition, VQ-VAE motion tokenization, cold-start SFT, GRPO) into a coherent two-stage framework.
Provides experiments on three datasets (HumanML3D, KIT-ML, BABEL) and reports standard text-to-motion metrics with confidence intervals.
The proposed RL Binding reward design is relatively simple and avoids training an additional human-preference model, potentially improving practicality.
Qualitative examples suggest improved generalization on out-of-distribution and compositional prompts.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing techniques—LLM-based chain-of-thought decomposition, VQ-VAE tokenization, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO with embedding-similarity rewards. The individual components are not new, and the paper does not convincingly demonstrate a fundamental advance over prior work.

The central claim of 'state-of-the-art performance' is only partially supported. On HumanML3D, Motion-R1 is not best on R-Precision@1 (tied with MotionLLM and below MoMask) and has substantially worse FID than MoMask (0.201 vs. 0.045) and MotionGPT-2 (0.191). On KIT-ML, MM-Dist is not best. The paper selectively emphasizes favorable metrics while downplaying weaker ones.

The RL reward relies on ground-truth motions during training (motion similarity reward). While this is not human preference annotation, it still requires paired motion data and encourages fitting the training trajectories, which may limit the claimed generalizability to truly novel text prompts.

The Decomposed CoT Data Engine is under-specified. There is little detail on prompt construction, data coverage, filtering statistics, possible failure modes, or how much the quality of generated CoT traces affects final performance. No human or automated validation of the reasoning traces is reported beyond a brief statement.

Ablation results are confusing and partly contradictory. For example, using both semantic and motion rewards without CoT yields much worse R-Precision than CoT alone or CoT plus one reward (0.365 vs. 0.482/0.483), which is not adequately explained. The statement that 'all ablated variants achieve comparable performance' is inconsistent with the large reported gaps.

The evaluation on BABEL is relegated to the appendix and compared mainly against older or less directly comparable baselines. The main paper's strong BABEL claims are therefore not fully substantiated in the primary experimental section.

The paper does not compare against the most relevant RL-based motion generation baselines (e.g., MotionRL, MotionCritic) under a unified setup, despite explicitly criticizing them. This weakens the empirical positioning.

Reproducibility is limited: code is promised but not available; key training details (data filtering thresholds, exact CoT generation and validation pipeline, reward scaling, prompt templates used for all datasets) are incomplete.

The writing has several errors and inconsistencies (e.g., 'embeded', 'mcan' for mean, inconsistent dataset counts, incorrect citation years), and the provided qualitative figures are low-resolution and not sufficient to substantiate motion quality claims.

strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant problem (text-to-motion generation) and connects recent trends (chain-of-thought-style reasoning, GRPO-based RL) to this domain.

The Decomposed CoT Data Engine is a reasonable automated pipeline that reduces reliance on hand-crafted intermediate supervision, and the overall two-stage (SFT cold-start + GRPO) training recipe is plausible.
Experiments span three widely-used benchmarks (HumanML3D, KIT-ML, BABEL), and an ablation over CoT, R_sem, and R_motion is provided.
Code is promised for release, and implementation details (group size, clipping, KL coefficient) are reported.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited and incremental: the paper essentially combines (a) LLM-based action decomposition/CoT prompting (a well-known idea, e.g., MotionAgent, and general R1-style pipelines) with (b) a fairly straightforward text/motion-embedding cosine-similarity reward under GRPO. Neither component is technically new, and the 'RL Binding' reward is a standard alignment metric rather than a novel mechanism.

The most directly relevant baselines for the central claim of 'simpler yet better RL'—MotionRL and MotionCritic—are criticized as 'over-engineered' but are conspicuously absent from all comparison tables. Without these comparisons the core motivational claim of the paper is unsupported.

The SOTA claims are selective and partly misleading. On HumanML3D, Motion-R1 attains FID 0.201 while MoMask reports 0.045—an order of magnitude worse—and R-Precision@1 (0.515) is not best (MoMask 0.521). The abstract/introduction emphasize a 3.5% MM-Dist gain and 'state-of-the-art performance' without acknowledging these substantial deficits, overstating the contribution.

The ablation analysis is internally inconsistent and mis-interpreted. The text states 'All ablated variants achieve comparable performance, showing the robustness of our design,' yet the first ablation row collapses to R-Precision 0.340 and FID 0.530 versus the full model's 0.515/0.201. The claim contradicts the table.

The ablation metrics are suspect: MModality for CoT-only and several variants is ~4–4.7 (far above the reported full-model 2.317 and above the ground-truth-like values typically seen), which is often a signature of degenerate/noisy outputs, yet this is not discussed.

Reproducibility and paper quality issues: the appendix figures are corrupted/garbled (repeated text such as 'The performance of the 2D model on the 2D model on the 3D model ...'), several references are mis-attributed or inconsistent (e.g., 'Guo et al. 2022c' cited as 'Back to MLP: A simple baseline for human motion prediction'), and 'MotionCoT' data is referenced without a clear definition. Section 4.1 says 'two widely-used benchmarks' and then lists three.

The Decomposed CoT Data Engine relies on DeepSeek-R1 for both generation and quality filtering; there is no independent validation of CoT quality, no measure of how often traces are rejected/regenerated, and no ablation of whether the CoT content actually matters versus simply more LLM-augmented text.

No quantitative results are reported for the out-of-distribution claims; the OOD generalization argument relies entirely on a few cherry-picked qualitative examples, which is insufficient for the paper's stated contributions.

strengths: The paper addresses two relevant problems in text-to-motion generation: capturing temporal/causal structure via decomposed chain-of-thought and simplifying RL-based optimization without costly preference annotations.
The Decomposed CoT Data Engine is a practical pipeline that synthesizes structured reasoning traces from LLMs, providing interpretable intermediate supervision and reducing manual annotation cost.

RL Binding integrates multi-modal text-motion alignment directly into GRPO rewards using motion-similarity, semantic-similarity, and format rewards; this is conceptually simple and avoids training separate preference models.

Experiments cover HumanML3D, KIT-ML, and BABEL, with standard metrics and confidence intervals. The method achieves strong results in several metrics, notably MM-Dist and R-Precision on HumanML3D, R-Precision/FID on KIT-ML, and all reported metrics on BABEL.
Ablation study attempts to isolate the contributions of decomposed CoT and the two RL reward terms, showing that combining them gives the best overall performance.
The paper is generally clear, includes implementation details, prompts, compute resources, and promises code release, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: the method combines existing components—LLM-generated chain-of-thought SFT, GRPO, and cosine-similarity rewards from pretrained T2M encoders—without introducing substantially new learning mechanisms or theoretical insights.

The evaluation lacks important RL-based text-to-motion baselines such as MotionRL and MotionCritic, despite the paper explicitly motivating its approach against complex RL methods. This weakens the empirical positioning.

The ablation study is incomplete: it does not include a no-CoT/no-RL SFT baseline, so the isolated benefit of decomposed CoT versus ordinary supervised fine-tuning is unclear. It also lacks ablations on the format reward, reward weighting, group size, and data-engine filtering thresholds.

The Decomposed CoT data quality is not rigorously validated. The same LLM family (DeepSeek-R1) is used both to generate and filter reasoning traces, and there is no human evaluation or quantitative analysis of reasoning faithfulness, leaving open the possibility of noisy or hallucinated decompositions.

The motion-similarity reward is computed against the paired ground-truth motion. While reasonable as a training signal, it may encourage reconstruction of a single GT trajectory rather than learning a truly one-to-many conditional distribution; this deserves deeper analysis and a control experiment.

Claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence: on HumanML3D the method is not state-of-the-art in FID and is only on par for R-Precision@1, yet the introduction/abstract give a broad impression of SOTA across key metrics. The paper should more carefully delimit where it is actually best.

Some writing/statements are inconsistent or confusing. For example, the ablation section says “All ablated variants achieve comparable performance” immediately before describing large performance drops, and the table formatting makes it difficult to parse which comparisons are meaningful.

The approach depends on external pretrained components (Qwen, DeepSeek-R1, T2M encoders) and LLM-generated data, which may raise reproducibility and data-licensing concerns that are not fully discussed.
